title: The contentious role of public art

paragraphs.text: Public art can be many things – a memorial in a park, a sculpture in a square or a mural on a wall. Whatever form it takes it can be indispensable to a city and its cultural life. While no-one visits Sydney, Australia, to see the memorial fountain in Hyde Park, they might visit the redeveloped port site of Barangaroo if it had artwork equivalent to that of Anish Kapoor’s Cloud Gate, which is located in a similar redeveloped site in Chicago. The price for a public artwork of that quality is high but if a council, investor or developer makes the right decision, it can be a drawcard that leads to significant economic gains.

Rain Oculus in Singapore’s upmarket commercial shopping precinct, Marina Bay Sands, is one such work. Created by US artist Ned Kahn, in collaboration with architect Moshe Safdie, it is a 23-metre diameter acrylic bowl of water forming a whirlpool that drops two storeys into another pool inside the building. While essentially a spectacle for tourists and a ‘thing to do’ when visiting Singapore, what’s fundamentally interesting about the work is that the art itself is integral to the architecture, design and plan of the centre. It is not an afterthought.

While not integrated to the same extent, American artist Jenny Holzer’s first Australian public art commission is close. It is a building that is distinctive high-rise, among a city of non-descript high-rises, thanks to its red steel braces that criss-cross the exterior. And then there’s Holzer’s artwork. Embedded in a steel column at the bottom of the building is I Stay (Ngaya ngalawa), a typographic LED* work featuring the writings of indigenous Australians in a scrolling series of text, visible from all directions.

Curator and art consultant Barbara Flynn set up a competition process with the developer to select the artwork. ‘Jenny came back with a work that was part of the fabric of the building. The other artists were not as closely aligned. I like leaving things up to the artist,’ she says. The result is that Holzer’s I Stay integrates not simply because it is part of the structure, but because it seeks to bring an emotional and even political intent to a building that may otherwise just be a vessel for workers.

Private developments in Sydney’s central business district, such as urban renewal projects requiring a masterplan, or developments over $10 million, are required to allocate a proportion of the budget, around one per cent, to public art. While it may be considered crucial for city-making, public art can also prompt fearful reactions from those who don’t like art that feels at odds with the environment or indeed the architecture itself.

Curator Virginia Wilson actively seeks artists who want to work with public space and architecture in entirely new ways, who are happy to cross mediums and leave the white walls of the studio. ‘Usually with the sort of budget involved you get to go to an artist and say “I’ve got X amount of money to spend. Have you got a vision that you can’t realise in a normal gallery space?”’

However, Wilson says that the ability to develop ideas, where the art is really integrated and embedded is ‘hard to achieve’, as no matter how early an artist may join a project, the architecture is already somewhat resolved. It is up to the developers to push for unique outcomes. Often, with high-end architects, the developer is quite engaged with the arts and wants it to be as interesting and innovative as the architecture.

Barbara Flynn agrees that a committed developer is key to a successful outcome. It would be a rare situation where the architect is not thrilled about the proposed art project, but it requires that there is a willing and visionary person within the development company for these projects to come to fruition.

Barangaroo is currently the largest development in Australia, with a budget for art and culture across the site of $40 million. Driving the outcomes at Barangaroo is senior development manager, Public Domain and Public Art, Annie Tennant. ‘What we decided to do is to aggregate the amount of money across the site. So instead of saying we are going to have 30 artworks, we will have 3 or 4 excellent artworks and a range of temporary programmes and art and cultural activations.’

The major work at Barangaroo will be the largest public art commission in Australia’s history, with the goal, as Tennant explains, to commission a work by an Australian or international artist that is a showstopper. ‘I can’t give you an amount of money at the moment, but one of our artworks is going to be a unique opportunity to put the City of Sydney on the map of art,’ she says.

While new developments, such as Barangaroo, benefit from the imposition of significant financial requirements with regard to art, ultimately it is the artists themselves who must initiate a broad approach to how they can integrate their work within a development. By exploring the use of materials and enlisting the help of engineers, artists can push the limits of what they propose, particularly at the submission stage. Perhaps more than architecture itself, great public art has the capacity to excite, confront and delight. It has the ability to make a city more dynamic and a new building or development a place you want to visit or inhabit
